evidence.description: Subsets, power sets and set operations
Cardinality via bijections and diagonal argument opening

sections.title: What this book helps you understand
sections.text: A bridge from calculating answers to explaining why mathematical statements hold. The selected pages develop sets, relations and functions as tools for precise reasoning, then use functions to compare finite and infinite collections.

sections.title: Central ideas
sections.text: Membership and containment answer different questions: an object may be an element without being a subset. A power set collects every subset; a finite n-element set has 2^n subsets. Equivalence relations formalize a chosen notion of sameness through reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity.

sections.title: How the explanation works
sections.text: Definitions are unpacked through small examples, diagrams and counterexamples. Subsets arise by choosing whether to include each element. Equivalence classes group related objects. Functions distinguish domain, codomain and actual range before injectivity and surjectivity are tested.

sections.title: Examples to keep in mind
sections.text: The book contrasts squaring R→R, which misses negative values and identifies opposite inputs, with cubing, which is bijective. Changing the squaring function’s codomain to nonnegative reals makes it onto. Thus a formula alone does not determine all function properties.

sections.title: Where it leads
sections.text: Equal cardinality means that a bijection exists, not that an endless counting process finishes. A systematic pairing matches natural numbers with integers. The diagonal argument then explains why no enumeration can capture all real numbers.

sections.title: How to use it here
sections.text: Check the chosen universe and codomain before operating on sets or functions. Read the explicit definitions, reconstruct one example yourself, and use the exercises to expose notation mistakes before moving to group actions.
